# JavaScript SEO pitfalls and fixes

Google's four common JavaScript indexing problems were content missing from the rendered HTML (the most common), # URLs, soft 404s and blocked resources; content goes missing when Googlebot cannot access the JavaScript, when it waits for a click or other DOM event, when it needs a disabled browser API, or when it appears too late. Single-page apps that return 200 for unknown routes create soft 404s, extending Day 1's soft 404 problem; Google's documented fixes are a real 404 or, where that is impractical, a JavaScript redirect to a URL that returns 404 or a noindex added with JavaScript, whereas removing a noindex with JavaScript does not work. Blocking script or API paths in robots.txt, on the page's host or on a separate API host, stops the renderer running them; Google recommended fast-rendering JavaScript, server-side or hybrid rendering, fallbacks, differential serving and polyfills, and called renderable content important today and tomorrow as AI systems increasingly ground answers, which extends Day 1's advice to keep content crawlable for AI tools. Community speakers added blind spots Google's documentation does not cover: prices and offers that differ between raw and rendered HTML, timeout placeholders that hit different pages each time, Content Security Policy blocks, pages that render blank while the raw HTML looks fine, and per-session-billed tools that also run for bot renders, which one speaker said can cost a high-traffic site thousands of euros a month. One community speaker urged putting everything you want AI systems to cite into server-rendered HTML, because some cannot render JavaScript yet. Day 3 put the delay in numbers: content added by JavaScript is typically seen by Google's indexing within a few hours and at worst within weeks, and Google's own speaker doubted that every URL gets rendered (said at the event). Author's view: Google's JavaScript guide says every page returning 200 is queued for rendering, but queued is not rendered, so critical content, links and meta tags belong in the server HTML. A second recording of Day 2 confirmed several of these points: a client-rendered page that renders empty for Google is seen as thin content before it becomes a soft 404, the product links in the debugging example sat behind onclick handlers, and when the JavaScript is not accessible parts of a page may render while the main content is absent. John Mueller added that when Google finds a noindex in the HTML it drops the page without processing its JavaScript, so robots meta tags belong in the HTML exactly as intended; Google's guide says it may skip rendering. In the retail example the rendered page promised a bigger newsletter discount than the raw HTML (the two recordings disagree on the figures), and a community speaker warned that a Content Security Policy blocking a video on a key landing page could hurt a purely online business badly. In the Day 1 Q&A, captured by an audio recording, Google said as a fun fact that JavaScript was used for the language-consolidation redirects in its own site migration, because it was the only option available to the person doing it. Author's view: Google's redirects guide says Google Search follows JavaScript redirects only after rendering and may never see one if rendering fails, so use them only when server-side or meta refresh redirects are impossible.

## What to do

- Ship everything indexing depends on in the server HTML, and server-render or pre-render the templates that must rank.
- Return a real 404 for unknown routes in single-page apps; where that is impractical, redirect with JavaScript to a URL that returns 404 or add noindex with JavaScript.
- Check robots.txt on every host a page loads scripts and APIs from, and carve out only what rendering needs, for example Disallow: /api/ with Allow: /api/products/.
- Diff raw and rendered HTML per template for prices, offer counts, links and meta tags, and scan recurring crawls for unresolved placeholders, rendering each URL more than once.
- Wrap permission-based APIs and WebGL in feature detection with fallbacks, and use differential serving and polyfills where Google's renderer lacks a feature.
- Compare the session counts that per-session-billed tools charge for with real user sessions, and load those tools only after a user interaction.

- **[Slide]** If an API folder must stay blocked in robots.txt, allow the endpoints that rendering needs, for example Disallow: /api/ together with Allow: /api/products/.

  <br><sub>`D2-C207` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Rebecca Yu) · consistent with Google docs · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec), [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) · Used by `DEV-REN-04`</sub>

- **[Slide]** robots.txt rules apply per host, so the rules in example.com/robots.txt do not apply at all to an API served from api.example.com.
  <br><sub>`D2-C209` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Rebecca Yu) · confirmed by Google docs · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Used by `DEV-SRV-04`, the glossary term *robots.txt*</sub>

- **[Stage]** On a product page whose data is fetched client-side, the rendering mistakes described can leave Google seeing no content at all while users still see the price and images.
  <br><sub>`D2-C211` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Rebecca Yu) · consistent with Google docs · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics)</sub>

- **[Stage]** In the speaker's product page example, three of the mistakes combine: product links behind onclick handlers keep the product detail pages hidden, the product API is blocked in robots.txt, and some content waits for a user interaction.
  <br><sub>`D2-C212` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Rebecca Yu)</sub>

- **[Stage]** A page that renders empty for Google, such as a client-side product page hit by these mistakes, is seen as thin content and ends up treated as a soft 404 even though users see a full page.

- **[Stage]** If JavaScript rendering fails, what Google indexes for a page differs from what the page shows once it is rendered.

- **[Stage]** Erin Sparling named server-side or hybrid rendering, fallbacks and not leaving placeholders in the DOM, among other measures, as ways to guard against failed JavaScript rendering.

## What Google's documentation says

- **[Docs]** Google's link best practices say Google can generally crawl a link only if it is an a element with an href attribute, and list routerLink without href, href on a span, onclick-only a elements and javascript: URLs as not recommended, while noting that Google may still attempt to parse them.
  <br><sub>`D2-C043` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, How is HTML interpreted · is the documentation · [Link best practices for Google](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/links-crawlable) · Used by `DEV-URL-01`, `DEV-URL-02`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's robots meta tag specification says data-nosnippet may be extracted both before and after rendering, so the attribute should not be added to or removed from existing elements with JavaScript.
  <br><sub>`D2-C079` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Controlling indexing · is the documentation · [Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag) · Used by `DEV-IDX-07`, `DEV-REN-05`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's meta tags documentation recommends avoiding JavaScript to inject or change meta tags whenever possible and testing the implementation thoroughly when it must be used.
  <br><sub>`D2-C107` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Controlling indexing · is the documentation · [meta tags and attributes that Google supports](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/special-tags) · Used by `DEV-REN-05`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's JavaScript SEO basics guide says that when Google encounters a noindex rule it may skip rendering and JavaScript execution, so using JavaScript to change or remove a noindex robots meta tag may not work as expected.
  > "it may skip rendering and JavaScript execution"
  <br><sub>`D2-C854` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Controlling indexing · is the documentation · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics) · Used by `DEV-REN-05`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's JavaScript SEO guide says Googlebot sends every page with a 200 HTTP status code to the rendering queue, whether or not it contains JavaScript, unless a robots meta tag or header tells Google not to index it, and Google uses the rendered HTML to index the page.
  <br><sub>`D2-C131` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · is the documentation · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics) · Extended by [D3-C676](../sessions/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) · Used by `DEV-REN-01`, the glossary term *Rendering*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's JavaScript guides say that when client-side routing makes a real 404 status impractical, a single-page app can avoid soft 404s by redirecting with JavaScript to a URL whose server returns 404, or by adding a robots noindex meta tag with JavaScript.
  <br><sub>`D2-C192` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · is the documentation · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics), [Fix Search-related JavaScript problems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/fix-search-javascript) · Used by `DEV-ERR-02`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google says its Web Rendering Service fetches the resources a page references through Googlebot, including JavaScript, CSS and XHR requests to APIs, but not images or videos.
  <br><sub>`D2-C206` · Search Central blog (3 December 2024), Search Central blog (31 March 2026) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · is the documentation · [Crawling December: The how and why of Googlebot crawling](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/12/crawling-december-resources), [Inside Googlebot: demystifying crawling, fetching, and the bytes we process](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/03/crawler-blog-post) · Used by `DEV-REN-04`</sub>

- **[Docs]** For effects that need WebGL, which Googlebot does not support, Google's guide to fixing JavaScript problems suggests skipping the effect or prerendering it with server-side rendering so that the content is accessible to Googlebot.
  <br><sub>`D2-C278` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript · is the documentation · [Fix Search-related JavaScript problems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/fix-search-javascript) · Used by `DEV-REN-08`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's JavaScript SEO basics recommends differential serving and polyfills when feature detection finds a missing browser API, and warns that some browser features cannot be polyfilled.
  > "We recommend using differential serving and polyfills if you feature-detect a missing browser API that you need."
  <br><sub>`D2-C280` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript · is the documentation · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics) · Used by `DEV-REN-08`</sub>

- **[Docs]** For client-side rendered single-page apps, where meaningful status codes can be impossible or impractical, Google's documentation gives two ways to avoid soft 404s: a JavaScript redirect to a URL that returns a 404 status, or a noindex robots meta tag added with JavaScript.
  <br><sub>`D2-C294` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript · is the documentation · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics), [Fix Search-related JavaScript problems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/fix-search-javascript) · Used by `DEV-ERR-02`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's introduction to robots.txt says unimportant image, script or style files may be blocked, but resources whose absence makes a page harder for Google to understand should not be blocked.
  <br><sub>`D2-C297` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript · is the documentation · [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) · Used by `DEV-REN-04`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's guide to fixing Search-related JavaScript problems says its Web Rendering Service keeps no state across page loads: local storage, session storage and HTTP cookies are cleared.
  <br><sub>`D2-C828` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript · is the documentation · [Fix Search-related JavaScript problems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/fix-search-javascript) · Used by `DEV-REN-06`</sub>

## Analysis

- **[Analysis]** Google's redirects guide says Google Search follows JavaScript location redirects only after rendering, may never see one if rendering fails, and should be used only when server-side or meta refresh redirects are impossible; its site move guide asks for server-side permanent redirects (301 or 308) where technically possible. The JavaScript in Google's own migration was a fallback ('my only option'), not a pattern to copy.
  <br><sub>`D1-C542` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, Q&A · [Redirects and Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/301-redirects), [How to move a site](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/site-move-with-url-changes) · Extends [D1-C541](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) · Used by `DEV-CAN-01`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Google's link-extraction slide put routerLink, href on a span, onclick-only links and javascript: URLs under 'can not extract', which is stricter than Google's link documentation saying Google may still try to parse them; either way they are not dependable links for discovery.
  <br><sub>`D2-C044` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, How is HTML interpreted</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Audit every template and JavaScript component that outputs links, such as navigation, pagination, filters and product tiles: each needs a real a element with an href, because onclick handlers, routerLink without href, href on a span and javascript: URLs leave the target pages without a link Google can reliably extract.
  <br><sub>`D2-C045` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, How is HTML interpreted</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Ship robots rules in the HTML the server sends and never rely on JavaScript to lift a noindex: Google may skip rendering a page that arrives with noindex, so the page can stay out of the index even if a script removes the tag later.
  <br><sub>`D2-C109` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Controlling indexing · Extended by [D2-C855](../sessions/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) · Used by `DEV-REN-05`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** On stage the rule was absolute (Google won't even process the JavaScript of a page served with noindex), while Google's guide says only that it may skip rendering; either way, a noindex in the served HTML must never be one that JavaScript is expected to lift.
  <br><sub>`D2-C855` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Controlling indexing · Extends [D2-C109](../sessions/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** For pages people are likely to ask an AI assistant about (product, pricing, documentation and policy pages), server-render the main content so a live, user-triggered read does not depend on client-side JavaScript finishing quickly.
  <br><sub>`D2-C125` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · Used by `DEV-PRF-02`, `DEV-REN-01`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The stage remark that content indexable without JavaScript can pass through without rendering does not mean such pages skip rendering, because Google's guide queues every 200 page for rendering; read it as: content already in the raw HTML does not depend on the slower rendering pass.
  <br><sub>`D2-C132` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Put everything indexing depends on (title, meta description, canonical, robots meta tag, main text and links) in the raw HTML so it is available without rendering, let JavaScript add enhancements only, and check the rendered HTML in URL Inspection for the rest.
  <br><sub>`D2-C133` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · Used by `DEV-REN-01`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Diff the raw and the rendered HTML of each key template for prices, offer counts, links and meta tags, and treat any difference in commercial data as a bug, because bots and users may get different versions.
  <br><sub>`D2-C148` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · Used by `DEV-MON-05`, `DEV-REN-07`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Add a check for unresolved template placeholders (such as {{brand}}, undefined or null) in rendered titles, meta descriptions and visible text to recurring crawls, and render the same URLs more than once, because such failures are intermittent.
  <br><sub>`D2-C154` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · Used by `DEV-MON-05`, `DEV-REN-06`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Compare the session counts that per-session-billed tools (chat, personalisation, testing, session replay) charge for with real user sessions, and load such tools only after a user interaction where they add no content that needs to be indexed.
  <br><sub>`D2-C165` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · Used by `DEV-PRF-03`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Check rendering per template rather than per URL: inspect one URL of each page type (product, category, article) in URL Inspection and confirm that the main content, prices and internal links appear in the rendered HTML.
  <br><sub>`D2-C179` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · Used by `DEV-MON-02`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** In a single-page app, let the server return 404 for unknown routes where possible; otherwise use one of the two client-side fixes Google documents for error views: a JavaScript redirect to a URL that returns 404, or a robots noindex added with JavaScript.
  <br><sub>`D2-C193` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Audit tabs, accordions and 'load more' lists for content fetched on click or scroll: put tab content in the initial DOM and hide it with CSS, trigger lazy loading with an Intersection Observer, and give long lists paginated URLs linked with `<a href>`.
  <br><sub>`D2-C203` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript</sub>

- **[Analysis]** A robots.txt carve-out works because Google applies the most specific matching rule, so Allow: /api/products/ beats Disallow: /api/ for product endpoints only; re-test a rendered page after every robots.txt change to script or API paths.
  <br><sub>`D2-C208` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · Extends [D1-C081](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** An API or CDN on its own host needs its own robots.txt check: a blanket Disallow there, or a robots.txt that returns 5xx errors, can stop Google fetching the data a page renders from.
  <br><sub>`D2-C210` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · Extends [D1-C074](../sessions/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-04`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Pages that embed third-party or AI-generated apps can share their fate, since an unhandled exception in the embedded code can break the host page; check the rendered HTML and JavaScript console output of such pages in Google's testing tools to make sure the host's own content still renders.
  <br><sub>`D2-C222` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · [Fix Search-related JavaScript problems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/fix-search-javascript) · Used by `DEV-REN-09`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Make sure robots.txt does not block the URLs from which the browser loads a fragment's assets (the gateway paths on the host page's origin, or the endpoint's own host if assets load from there), because Google does not render JavaScript from blocked files and robots.txt rules apply per host.
  <br><sub>`D2-C245` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec), [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Treat the 10,000-pixel viewport as a safety margin, not a target: load lazy content when it enters the viewport (Intersection Observer or native lazy loading, never scroll listeners), and give infinite-scroll content paginated URLs linked with `<a href>` so anything below the first rendered screen stays reachable.
  <br><sub>`D2-C275` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Wrap permission-based features (location, payments, camera) and WebGL effects in feature detection with a fallback, so the main content renders when the API is missing or the permission is declined; never make indexable content wait for a permission prompt.
  <br><sub>`D2-C282` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript · Used by `DEV-REN-08`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Audit a single-page app by searching both the templates and the rendered HTML for href="#..." routes, `<a>` elements without href and onclick navigation; every view that should rank needs an `<a href>` link to a real path.
  <br><sub>`D2-C290` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript</sub>

- **[Analysis]** After moving to real paths, set the server or hosting rewrite rules so a direct request to every valid path returns 200 with the content (ideally server-rendered) and an unknown path returns a 404 status, which removes client-side soft 404s at the source.
  <br><sub>`D2-C295` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript · Used by `DEV-ERR-02`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Check robots.txt for Disallow rules covering JavaScript bundles, build folders or API endpoints the page calls while rendering, including on separate API or CDN hostnames with their own robots.txt, then confirm in URL Inspection's live test that the rendered HTML contains the main content.
  <br><sub>`D2-C298` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript</sub>

- **[Analysis]** With a headless CMS, choose the rendering per template before launch (server-rendered or pre-rendered for pages that must rank), and make any agent-built test suite assert that the main content and `<a href>` links are present in the rendered HTML.
  <br><sub>`D2-C305` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Return real error status codes for error states, 404 or 410 for missing content and 503 for outages such as a failed database connection, also in single-page apps; a 200 page whose main content is only an error message is treated as a soft 404 even when header and navigation look normal.
  <br><sub>`D2-C342` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Understanding what's on a page · Used by `DEV-ERR-03`, `DEV-SRV-03`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Put critical content, links and meta tags in the server HTML: content that needs JavaScript reaches indexing only after rendering, usually within hours but sometimes weeks, and even Google's own speaker doubted that every URL gets rendered.
  <br><sub>`D3-C630` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, How long does it take to..?</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The stage doubt that every URL gets rendered sits beside Google's JavaScript guide, which says every page with a 200 status is queued for rendering unless a robots rule blocks indexing: queued is not the same as rendered, so do not rely on rendering for critical content.
  <br><sub>`D3-C676` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, How long does it take to..? · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics) · Extends [D2-C131](../sessions/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Used by `DEV-REN-01`</sub>

## Built on these claims

The items of the developer and content kits that rest on this topic's claims.

- Requirement `DEV-CAN-01`: Use permanent server-side redirects (301 or 308) for moved URLs, straight to the final URL
- Requirement `DEV-CAN-02`: Serve one host over HTTPS with a valid certificate and redirect every other origin to it
- Requirement `DEV-ERR-02`: Return a real 404 for unknown routes in single-page apps, or use a documented client-side fallback
- Requirement `DEV-ERR-03`: Never serve error states, empty results or failed data loads with a 200 status
- Requirement `DEV-HTM-03`: Give every indexable page a unique, descriptive title element in the server HTML
- Requirement `DEV-IDX-07`: Use data-nosnippet on a span, div or section to keep one detail out of snippets
- Requirement `DEV-MON-02`: Render every template in a headless browser before release and check it in URL Inspection right after
- Requirement `DEV-MON-05`: Run recurring rendering checks: raw versus rendered HTML, placeholders and console errors
- Requirement `DEV-MON-10`: Plan releases and fixes around Google's processing times, and judge results only after them
- Requirement `DEV-PRF-02`: Make JavaScript-generated content render quickly
- Requirement `DEV-PRF-03`: Load per-session-billed third-party tools only after a user interaction
- Requirement `DEV-REN-01`: Server-render the main content and everything indexing depends on (SSR, static generation or hybrid)
- Requirement `DEV-REN-02`: Have all indexable content in the DOM after load, without clicks, typing or scrolling
- Requirement `DEV-REN-03`: Lazy-load with native lazy loading or an IntersectionObserver, never with scroll events
- Requirement `DEV-REN-04`: Do not block JavaScript, CSS or API endpoints that pages need for rendering in robots.txt
- Requirement `DEV-REN-05`: Do not add, change or remove robots meta tags with JavaScript
- Requirement `DEV-REN-06`: Make rendering robust: no slow API dependencies and no unresolved placeholders
- Requirement `DEV-REN-07`: Keep prices, offer counts and other commercial data identical in raw and rendered HTML
- Requirement `DEV-REN-08`: Feature-detect permission-based APIs and WebGL, and render the content without them
- Requirement `DEV-REN-09`: Monitor JavaScript console errors and Content Security Policy violations on key templates
- Requirement `DEV-SRV-03`: Answer planned maintenance and short outages with 503, for a day or two at most
- Requirement `DEV-SRV-04`: Keep robots.txt reachable on every host: 200 with rules, or 404 if there are none
- Requirement `DEV-URL-01`: Make every navigational link an `<a>` element whose href holds a real URL
- Requirement `DEV-URL-02`: Do not navigate with onclick handlers, javascript: URLs, routerLink without href or # pseudo-links
- Requirement `DEV-URL-03`: Route single-page apps with the History API and real paths, not # fragments

- Glossary term *Lazy loading*
- Glossary term *Rendering*
- Glossary term *robots.txt*
- Glossary term *Single-page app (SPA)*
